history.check: Skill coverage audited against the captured port lessons; one gap found and closed
history.detail: Audited all four reusable skills by grepping each captured lesson against the skill corpus rather than asserting coverage. Eleven lessons were present: source encoding, host toolchain assertion, LIB/atlmfc purity roots, byte-level evidence method, foreign-architecture negative control, ARM64X code-map scanning, required Plugins\Exporter directory, rejected x64 CRT, breakpoint width, alignment, and architecture-dependent payloads. One lesson had zero coverage: the DIA SDK dependency. msdia140.dll is a genuine shipped ARM64 dependency of this port that is delivered by the Visual Studio DIA SDK rather than by any package feed, so a manifest-only audit misses it, and the SDK default bin directory holds the x86 build under a file name identical to the arm64 one. Closed by adding the lesson to native-dependency-analysis SKILL.md judgment rules and references/archive-audit.md, plus detection rule DEP-0003 with a positive fixture copying from bin and a negative fixture copying from bin\arm64. The first regex required the literal "DIA SDK" on the same line and scored 67 percent recall, which is how the fixture caught it; it was corrected to the directory shape. Separately, appending this entry via a PowerShell ConvertTo-Json round trip silently rewrote 15 existing timestamps from .000+03:00 to +03:00, so the file was restored byte-identically and the entry inserted textually; a serializer round trip is not a safe way to amend an evidence record. Post-change: evals 4 of 4 skills at 100 percent recall and 0 percent false positives, contracts 47 of 47, all three run directories VALID.

history.check: All four agents updated with the lessons this port produced

It also gains the two-valid-encoding-repairs rule, the byte-safe reader rule, the DIA SDK copy path, the negative-control run, and explicit exclusion recording. port-review gains foreignArchRefusal and hostToolchainSingle as hard gates, the instruction to turn its adversarial lens on its own gates, product-identity verification for a repository reporting fork=false, and retraction discipline. winport gains the matched-pair requirement, the rule that a falsely-green run stays in history as a failure, the rule that evidence is amended textually rather than through a serializer round trip, and intake only from immutable references.

history.check: Remaining capability gap recorded rather than glossed
history.detail: The agents still cannot repeat this port unaided, and the gap is recorded here so it is not mistaken for completeness. Of twelve skills the agents reference by name, five exist: build-retarget, port-packaging, arm64-correctness, native-dependency-analysis, and the security-review subagent. Seven do not: repo-structure, linux-dependency-analysis, build-system-analysis, ui-framework-analysis, arm64-readiness, port-completeness, and windows-nativeness. arm64-readiness is the most consequential because port-analysis routes its entire ARM64 detection pass through it; the agent degrades to doing that detection inline, which is exactly the improvisation the skill set exists to remove. Beyond skills, two hard prerequisites are not knowledge at all and cannot be captured as such: native ARM64 execution requires windows-11-arm hardware or a runner, and the ARM64 compiler component must be installed, neither of which any agent can provide for itself. Finally, one mechanism remains unexplained and unasserted: why a 32-bit MSBuild selects HostX86 on a runner reporting ARM64.

history.check: arm64-readiness and port-completeness authored as real skills
history.detail: The two missing skills on the critical path for repeating this port now exist rather than being named by agents that could not load them. arm64-readiness owns the pre-port detection pass that port-analysis routes its entire ARM64 row through, with seven RDY rules covering x86 SIMD intrinsics, inline assembly that MSVC cannot compile for ARM64 at all, x86 architecture macros with no answering branch, dependency payloads declared only for x86 and x64, opcode literals written into another process, C++/CLI requiring an explicit disposition, and hard-coded HostX86 or HostX64 toolchain paths. port-completeness owns the silent-loss pass that port-migration and port-review both route through, with four CMP rules covering undocumented platform exclusions, disabled or filtered tests, functionality stubbed behind an architecture guard, and test steps gated on an exit code alone. Both carry the measured lessons of this workstream rather than generic advice: the 0xCC versus BRK #0 payload distinction, the ThirdParty package that shipped only x86-windows and x64-windows, the TestCppCli exclusion that separated a 215-test line from a 216-test line, and the rule that absent evidence is not clean evidence. Five new structured detectors were added to the eval harness to support them. All six skills scan at 100 percent recall and 0 percent false positives.

history.check: New rules mutation-tested, and the eval harness itself repaired
history.detail: Both new skills passed on the first run, which by the rule this workstream encodes is precisely when a gate deserves distrust, so each negative control was mutation-tested by removing exactly the property that exonerates it. Every one of the six mutations produced new findings, proving the negative controls are genuine near-misses rather than vacuous passes: removing the ARM64 branch made 0xCC a finding again, removing the arm64 payload re-fired the dependency rule, restoring HostX64 re-fired the host rule, stripping the recorded reason re-fired the exclusion rule, replacing the ARM64 implementation with a TODO re-fired the stub rule, and deleting the executed-count assertion re-fired the vacuous-success rule. The suite nevertheless still reported PASS on all six, because the harness tolerated a false-positive rate of up to 20 percent and a small corpus keeps one or two spurious findings under that ceiling. That is a gate unable to fail its author, found by measurement rather than by reading. The harness now treats any fixture declared with no expected findings as absolute: a negative control must observe exactly zero findings, and aggregate tolerance no longer applies there. Under the stricter rule the four pre-existing skills still pass unchanged, so no existing false positive was being masked, and all six mutations are now killed.

history.check: Stated reason for lacy's absence from ports/ corrected to the review verdict, not the missing fork
history.detail: ports/README.md previously said lacy has no entry because no fork exists. That was true but understated, and understatement here invites precisely the wrong repair: fork upstream, apply the patch, pin the result, thereby pinning a commit nobody measured and defeating the rule the directory exists to enforce. The governing reason is the verdict. runs/lacy-2026-08-14 records status blocked-external and verdict REVISE with REV-0004 unresolved; arm64Purity, buildGreen and planCompleteness pass, runtimeValidated fails, packaging fails as advisory and performance is not-run. Nothing was cross-compiled wrong, the binary is genuinely ARM64 by winport-scan at 2 of 2 modules native; it has simply never been executed, because no ARM64 device was available and configured-but-unexecuted CI is not runtime evidence. There are therefore no runner links for lacy at all, passing or failing, and a search of the run directory for any actions/runs reference confirms none is recorded. The port commit 90c7b83d6d74268ede895f1e91ab9642ce80ffd1 exists in no remote, upstream returning HTTP 422, and survives only as a 7-commit patch against upstream dca3410, which does resolve. The entry criterion for ports/ is now stated explicitly as two conditions, a repository that exists and a commit this repository measured and accepted, with the second identified as the one that matters more.

history.check: Runtime proof surfaced on the repository front page instead of only in structured evidence
history.detail: The CI proof for the port was already recorded correctly but was not discoverable: run links lived in handoff.json, build.json and prose partway down two READMEs, so a visitor landing on the front page saw no evidence at all. README.md now opens with a Proof section immediately after the install commands. It leads with run 32357865925, the run whose display title is Port OpenCppCoverage to native Windows ARM64, and gives its three jobs with runner labels: Native Windows ARM64 on windows-11-arm, plus x64 and x86 compatibility on windows-2022, all success. Each row links the job log committed under runs/opencppcoverage-2026-08-19/evidence/, and the three job ids in those filenames, 96390868682, 96390868985 and 96390869040, were confirmed against the Actions API to be the real job ids for that run rather than filenames that merely look plausible. The section states why a green Arm64 run is insufficient on its own, since an x64 binary also runs there under emulation, and links run 32396073242 which asserts both directions, must run on windows-11-arm and must NOT run on windows-2022 or windows-latest, plus run 32361171722 which executes the downloaded release asset rather than a rebuild. A drafting error was caught and corrected before commit: the text claimed the three jobs were handoff.evidence[0..6], but those seven records all derive from the single native Arm64 log and are seven evidence kinds, three build, two test, one runtime and one package. The corrected wording was then verified, as was integrity of the artifact itself: the committed native Arm64 log hashes to af70ba3a6d7402d092daa034b0590f50402d20c8507bdd6bd5eab93619f77603, exactly the sha256 recorded in handoff.json, at 540071 bytes matching the recorded size, so a substituted log would fail the contract rather than pass quietly. Every relative link in the new section was resolved on disk, 7 of 7 present.
